1H (Number Theory)

Words: 114 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 114
1H OurBigBook.com
For an odd prime p, the Legendre symbol (a/p) is zero if p∣a, one if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and minus one otherwise. By Gauss lemma, (2/p)=(−1)N, where N counts those least positive residues of 2,4,…,p−1 which exceed p/2. They correspond to integers j>p/4 among 1≤j≤(p−1)/2, hence
N=2p−1​−⌊4p​⌋.
(1)
For p≡1,3,5,7(mod8), its parity is respectively 0,1,1,0, the same as that of (p2−1)/8. Therefore
(p2​)=(−1)(p2−1)/8.​
(2)
Use multiplicativity and quadratic reciprocity for the requested composite numerator. Since 91=7⋅13,
(1677​)=−(7167​)=−(7−1​)=1,(16713​)=(1311​)=(112​)=−1.
(3)
The first reciprocity sign is negative because both primes are 3(mod4); the subsequent signs are positive because one prime is 1(mod4). Thus (91/167)=−1.

2F (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 111 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 111
2F OurBigBook.com
The hyperbolic cosine has the absolutely convergent expansion cosh(1/2)=∑k≥0​1/[4k(2k)!]. Suppose its value were a rational a/b, with b>0. For sufficiently large N, b∣(2N)!. Multiplying by 4N(2N)! makes the assumed value an integer, and every term of the partial sum through k=N is also an integer. Their difference is the positive remainder
RN​=∑j=1∞​4j(2N+2j)!(2N)!​.
(4)
Let q=[4(2N+1)(2N+2)]−1. Every new pair of factorial factors is at least (2N+1)(2N+2), so 0<RN​≤∑j≥1​qj=q/(1−q)<1 for N≥1. No integer lies strictly between zero and one. This contradiction proves cosh(1/2) is irrational. The argument uses a finite integer partial sum and a controlled tail; it does not infer irrationality merely from an infinite expansion.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 331 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 331
3G OurBigBook.com
A discrete subgroup of the Euclidean isometry group has the identity isolated in the group topology. Equivalently, no sequence of distinct group elements converges to the identity; translating neighbourhoods then isolates every element. Such a subgroup is closed, and its intersection with any compact subset is finite: otherwise two elements of a convergent sequence would have quotient tending to the identity.
Write each Euclidean isometry uniquely as x↦Qx+b, Q∈O(2). Its linear part gives the group homomorphism G→O(2), since the linear part of a composite is the product of the linear parts. Its kernel is exactly the translation subgroup GT​. The translation vectors form a discrete additive subgroup L⊂R2.
If L={0}, choose a shortest nonzero vector a, possible by discreteness and finiteness in compact balls. On its line, Euclidean division of a scalar coefficient by one proves L∩Ra=Za: a nonzero remainder would be shorter than a. If all vectors are collinear, this finishes the proof. Otherwise orient the perpendicular coordinate so some vector has positive height. Reduce every vector's component along a modulo a into a bounded interval. Among vectors with positive height at most that of a chosen vector, these reduced representatives lie in a compact rectangle and are finite. Choose b with the smallest such positive height. Subtracting an integer multiple of b from any vector of L reduces its height into [0,b⊥​); minimality makes the remainder's height zero, so it is an integer multiple of a. Thus
L={0},Za,or Za+Zb with a,b linearly independent.​
(5)
This derives the rank-at-most-two translation lattice rather than assuming every discrete subgroup of the plane is a full lattice.
Two examples with GT​≅Z are the group generated by T(x,y)=(x+1,y) alone, and the infinite dihedral group generated by T together with R(x,y)=(−x,y). The latter has RTR=T−1; its elements are translations Tk and reflections TkR, whose mirror lines are x=k/2. The first group preserves the orientation of every translated motif; the second also reverses it across these mirrors.

4J (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 173 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 173
4J OurBigBook.com
Shannon-Fano coding orders symbols by decreasing probability and recursively splits each consecutive block into two groups with probability totals as close as possible, appending bits zero and one. Huffman coding instead repeatedly merges the two least probable nodes, constructs a binary tree upwards, and then assigns the branch bits. Both yield prefix codes, so a concatenation can be decoded without separators; Huffman coding minimizes expected length among binary prefix codes.
For the specified probabilities, the first Shannon-Fano coding split is {μ1​} of mass 0.45 versus the remaining mass 0.55. Split the latter into {μ2​} of mass 0.25 and {μ3​,μ4​,μ5​} of mass 0.30, and then split off μ3​. One resulting code is
μ1​:0,μ2​:10,μ3​:110,μ4​:1110,μ5​:1111.​
(6)
Its expected word length is 0.45+2(0.25)+3(0.20)+4(0.05+0.05)=1.95 bits​.
The Huffman coding merges are 0.05+0.05=0.10, 0.10+0.20=0.30, 0.25+0.30=0.55, and 0.45+0.55=1. Reading the resulting tree gives the same code lengths 1,2,3,4,4, and it may give exactly the displayed code if the branch bits are chosen accordingly. Its expected length is also 1.95 bits. The methods agree here; their agreement on this particular distribution is not a claim that the two procedures always coincide.

Differentiate the normalization of the exponential family density with respect to θi​, assuming the regularity that permits differentiation under its integral. The density derivative is f(yi​∣θi​,ϕ)[yi​−b′(θi​)]/ϕ. Consequently
0=ϕ1​(EYi​−b′(θi​)),μi​=b′(θi​).​
(7)
Differentiating the expectation once more gives dμi​/dθi​=Var(Yi​)/ϕ, so
Vi​=Var(Yi​)=ϕb′′(θi​).​
(8)
The log-likelihood derivative with respect to θi​ is (yi​−μi​)/ϕ. For the generalized linear model with linear predictor ηi​=βTxi​=g(μi​), the chain rule gives
dμi​dθi​​=b′′(θi​)1​,∂β∂μi​​=g′(μi​)xi​​.
(9)
Using independence to add the log-likelihood contributions proves the score function
∂β∂ℓ​=i=1∑n​g′(μi​)Vi​(yi​−μi​)xi​​.​
(10)
Here Vi​ includes the dispersion parameter ϕ. Defining instead a unit-dispersion variance function b′′(θi​) would require retaining an explicit ϕ in the denominator.

a OurBigBook.com
The nullclines are x=f(y) and y=g(x), both decreasing curves in the positive quadrant. To their left/right the horizontal velocity is respectively positive/negative; below/above the second nullcline the vertical velocity is positive/negative. Bounded positive synthesis functions give an inward-pointing sufficiently large rectangle, while the axes point into the quadrant. More directly, put H(x)=f(g(x))−x: H(0)>0, and H(x)<0 for large enough x. Continuity therefore gives a positive equilibrium.
At an equilibrium, the Jacobian matrix is J=(−1g′(x∗​)​f′(y∗​)−1​), with eigenvalues −1±f′(y∗​)g′(x∗​)​. Its logarithmic-slope product is
f(y∗​)y∗​f′(y∗​)​g(x∗​)x∗​g′(x∗​)​=f′(y∗​)g′(x∗​),
(11)
because f(y∗​)=x∗​ and g(x∗​)=y∗​. Thus a product exceeding one makes this equilibrium a saddle and gives H′(x∗​)>0. Immediately on its left H<0, and immediately on its right H>0. Since H(0)>0 and H is eventually negative, there must be other roots on both sides, crossing in the attracting direction. For simple roots those have H′<0, hence two negative Jacobian eigenvalues: the saddle separates at least two stable steady-state alternatives. The divergence is −2, so periodic attractors cannot replace these equilibria in a bounded planar region. Nongeneric flat crossings or intervals of equilibria require a nonlinear stability interpretation; the strict saddle inequality alone does not guarantee that every other root is hyperbolic. This is the usual mutual repression stability criterion behind bistability.
The conclusion also has a nonlinear trapping justification. Choose l<u on the left of the saddle with H(l)>0>H(u); such endpoints exist by the signs just proved. The rectangle [l,u]×[g(u),g(l)] is forward invariant: on the vertical edges, f(y)−l≥f(g(l))−l>0 and f(y)−u≤f(g(u))−u<0, while the horizontal-edge velocities point inward or are tangent. The same construction on the right of the saddle gives a second disjoint trapping rectangle. Each contains a nonempty compact attracting invariant set, obtained by intersecting its nested forward images; strict vertical inwardness also rules out invariant boundary trajectories. If a downward crossing is isolated, endpoints can be taken arbitrarily close to it, proving nonlinear stability, and the absence of periodic orbits makes nearby trajectories converge to that equilibrium. Intervals of equilibria instead give attracting alternatives consisting of families, so bounded monotone functions without nondegeneracy do not necessarily produce two isolated hyperbolic attractors.

b OurBigBook.com
At a positive equilibrium of the bounded Hill model, the mutual repression stability criterion becomes
K=mn1+ymym​1+xnxn​>1.
(12)
Thus mn>1 is necessary. Because the same λ is imposed in both synthesis functions, it is not sufficient for arbitrary unequal positive exponents. The additional equilibrium constraint is
x(1+ym)=y(1+xn),y1​+ym−1=x1​+xn−1.
(13)
Here is an exact criterion for all the printed exponent choices, including nonintegers. If m>1 and n>1, multistability is possible: for large λ the intermediate equilibrium satisfies x∼λ(m−1)/(mn−1), y∼λ(n−1)/(mn−1), so both increase without bound and K→mn>1. These asymptotics follow by balancing xym∼λ and yxn∼λ; the limiting two algebraic equations have a nonsingular log-Jacobian when mn=1, so a nearby exact equilibrium exists for large λ. If both exponents are at most one, K<1 everywhere and multistability is impossible.
For the remaining case, interchange x,y if necessary so 0<m≤1<n. For each x>0, let Y(x)>0 be the unique solution of
Y−1+Ym−1=x−1+xn−1,
(14)
which exists because the left side is strictly decreasing; for m=1 the right side always exceeds one. Define
Km,n​(x)=(1+xn)(1+Y(x)m)mnxnY(x)m​.
(15)
Then the exact answer for this remaining range is
multistability for some common λ ⟺ x>0max​Km,n​(x)>1.​
(16)
This is a one-variable test depending only on m,n, with no unknown λ. To prove it, parameterize all equilibria by λ(x)=x(1+Y(x)m). Implicit differentiation gives
λ′(x)=1−mYm/(1+Ym)(1+Ym)(1−Km,n​(x))​.
(17)
The denominator is positive, and λ(x) goes from zero to infinity as x goes from zero to infinity. A negative-slope portion therefore forces two folds and an interval of three equilibria, with two attracting branches. If K≤1 everywhere, λ is strictly increasing apart from possible isolated stationary points, so there is only one equilibrium for each λ. This is the common-strength Hill repression criterion.
For illustration and a closed test on the boundary m=1, Y=x/(1+xn−x) and
maxK1,n​=4n(n−1)2​(n−1n+1​)(n+1)/n,n>1,
(18)
obtained at xn=(n+1)/(n−1). In particular (m,n)=(1,2) has mn>1 but maximum 33​/8<1, so it cannot be multistable. For positive integer exponents the allowed choices simplify to both exponents at least two, or one equal to one and the other at least four. For arbitrary real exponents the preceding exact criterion is needed; replacing it by mn>1 would discard the common-strength constraint.
The unbounded power laws behave differently. Combining their equilibrium equations gives x1−mn=λ1−m. If mn=1, there is exactly one positive equilibrium,
x=λ(1−m)/(1−mn),y=λ(1−n)/(1−mn).
(19)
Its slope product is exactly mn, so it is attracting if mn<1 and a saddle if mn>1, but there are never two isolated attracting equilibria. If mn=1, equilibria exist only when λ1−m=1; when this holds there is a whole curve of equilibria, with a zero tangent eigenvalue and transverse eigenvalue −2. This includes m=n=1, xy=λ, for every λ. A neutrally degenerate continuum is not bistability between isolated attractors. Thus these power laws do not generate ordinary multistability; boundedness was essential to the outer-root argument in part (a).

7B (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 187 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 187
7B OurBigBook.com
The Bendixson-Dulac criterion says that if a C1 planar field admits a C1 multiplier B on a simply connected region such that ∇⋅(Bf) has one strict sign there, no nonconstant periodic orbit lies wholly in that region. The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem says that a nonempty compact omega-limit set of a planar C1 flow which contains no equilibria is a periodic orbit.
For μ<0, the divergence of the given field is μ−2x2−3y2<0 throughout the plane. Taking B=1 proves there are no periodic orbits.
For μ>0, use E=(x2+y2)/2. Along trajectories,
E˙=xx˙+yy˙​=y2(μ−2x2−y2).
(20)
On a circle r=r−​ with 2r−2​<μ the radial flow is outward or tangent, and on a circle r=r+​ with r+2​>μ it is inward or tangent. Their intervening closed annulus is positively invariant. At the tangent points y=0, the field has y˙​=−x=0, so no equilibrium sits on its boundaries. Indeed the only equilibrium is the origin, excluded from the annulus. Every forward trajectory in the annulus has a nonempty compact omega-limit set without equilibria. The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem consequently proves at least one periodic orbit exists for every μ>0. No claim of uniqueness follows from this trapping argument.

8A (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 227 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 227
8A OurBigBook.com
A Papperitz symbol records the three regular singular points of a second-order Fuchsian differential equation and the two local exponents at each. Exponents at infinity refer to solutions behaving as z−γ, that is, to powers of the local coordinate 1/z. Their sum satisfies the Fuchs relation: the six exponents add to one. The symbol represents the two-dimensional solution space, not one normalized solution by itself.
The specified exponents give the Gauss hypergeometric equation
z(1−z)u′′+[c−(a+b+1)z]u′−abu=0.
(21)
Set d=c−a−b and let v=F(c−a,c−b;c;z). Its equation is
z(1−z)v′′+[c−(2c−a−b+1)z]v′−(c−a)(c−b)v=0.
(22)
For u=(1−z)dv, differentiation gives u′=(1−z)d[v′−dv/(1−z)] and u′′=(1−z)d[v′′−2dv′/(1−z)+d(d−1)v/(1−z)2]. Substitution into the first equation leaves (1−z)d times exactly the second equation: its v′ coefficient is c−(a+b+1+2d)z, and its v coefficient simplifies to −(c−a)(c−b). Hence u solves the same equation as F(a,b;c;z).
The symbol gives the same check geometrically: multiplication by (1−z)d shifts the exponents at one from {0,−d} to {d,0} and those at infinity from {c−a,c−b} to {b,a}; it does not change the exponents at zero. Choose the branch with (1−0)d=1. Then u is analytic at zero and u(0)=1. For c∈/{0,−1,−2,…} the analytic recurrence uniquely determines this normalized solution, proving
F(a,b;c;z)=(1−z)c−a−bF(c−a,c−b;c;z).​
(23)
The identity continues wherever both sides are defined with compatible branches. At exceptional parameters where the stated normalization does not uniquely define an analytic function, a parameter-continuation convention is needed; the generic proof does not silently assume uniqueness there. This is Euler's hypergeometric transformation.

a OurBigBook.com
For dilute nonrelativistic nucleons in thermal equilibrium, their Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution gives nj​=gj​(mj​kT/2πℏ2)3/2exp[(μj​−mj​c2)/kT]. The neutron and proton spin degeneracies are equal, and their mass prefactor ratio is nearly one. Thus
np​nn​​≃exp[kTμn​−μp​−Q​].
(25)
Weak reaction equilibrium imposes μn​+μνe​​=μp​+μe​. Charge neutrality in an electron-positron plasma, together with the small baryon asymmetry, makes μe​/kT very small. Assuming negligible neutrino lepton asymmetry also makes μνe​​/kT small. Hence the difference, rather than the absolute baryon chemical potentials, is negligible, yielding
nn​/np​≃e−Q/kT.​
(26)
A large neutrino chemical potential would invalidate this last approximation; it is an assumption about the lepton asymmetry, not a general rule that baryonic chemical potentials vanish.

The weak-conversion rate per expansion time falls as T3. Below the stated threshold it becomes less than one, so neutron-proton interconversion cannot track the rapidly changing equilibrium ratio: cosmological weak freeze-out occurs. Free neutrons subsequently decay, reducing their abundance until nuclei can survive photodissociation. Once the deuterium bottleneck is passed, nuclear reactions rapidly assemble neutrons into the strongly bound helium-4 nucleus. The short available time, low density and missing stable mass-five and mass-eight nuclei impede extensive production of heavier nuclei, leaving nearly all surviving neutrons in helium.
If r=nn​/np​ just before helium formation, each helium nucleus uses two neutrons and two protons, so nHe​=nn​/2. Neglecting binding-energy corrections to nuclear masses,
Y4He​=nn​+np​4(nn​/2)​=1+r2r​=92​≃0.222(r=1/8).​
(27)
The remaining protons mainly become hydrogen. Counting all four helium nucleons, rather than only the captured neutrons, is essential to this mass fraction.

c

Words: 175 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 175
c OurBigBook.com
If the weak-rate coefficient is reduced, equality with the expansion rate occurs at a higher temperature, since ΓW​/H scales as that coefficient times T3. The freeze-out temperature and interaction strength relation is Tf​∝CW−1/3​. The frozen neutron-to-proton ratio is then closer to one, so the primordial helium mass fraction increases, potentially approaching unity if nearly equal numbers survive to nucleosynthesis. If the same weaker interaction also slows free-neutron decay, it reinforces this trend; changing conversion rates alone would instead require a separate treatment of the decay interval.
Less primordial hydrogen means less hydrogen fuel and, for otherwise comparable stellar physics, helium enrichment raises the mean molecular weight, tending to make a fixed-mass star hotter and more luminous and to shorten its hydrogen-burning lifetime. A genuinely weaker weak interaction also changes proton-proton fusion itself, so a quantitative lifetime cannot be inferred from composition alone. Much less hydrogen and fewer long-lived suitable stars would alter planet formation, water availability and the timescales needed for life on Earth. These are physical implications of the changed initial composition, not a numerical prediction of habitability from the helium fraction alone.

11F OurBigBook.com
The triangular-grid form is Sperner's lemma: subdivide a triangle into small triangles meeting edge to edge, label its vertices 1,2,3, and forbid label i on the side opposite corner i. The corner labels are thereby forced. An odd number of small triangles, in particular at least one, carry all three labels.
Here is the parity proof. Count incidences of a small triangle with an edge whose endpoint labels are 1,2. On the outer boundary these edges occur only on the side joining corners 1,2; traversing that side begins with label one and ends with label two, so the number of changes of label is odd. Interior edges contribute twice to the incidence count. A small triangle with all three labels contributes once; a triangle having only labels one and two contributes twice if it has both, and all other triangles contribute zero. Reduction modulo two therefore proves the assertion.
To obtain the continuous Brouwer fixed-point theorem on the triangle, use barycentric coordinates and a continuous map F from the triangle to itself. If a grid vertex is not already fixed, label it by an index i with xi​>Fi​(x), which exists since both coordinate sums are one. A point on the side xi​=0 cannot receive label i, so the discrete lemma applies. On successively finer grids take a fully labelled small triangle. Compactness gives a subsequence converging to one point x; all three vertices converge to it because the mesh tends to zero. Passing to the limit in the three label inequalities gives xi​≥Fi​(x) for every i. Equal coordinate sums force equality throughout, hence F(x)=x.
A closed disk is homeomorphic to a triangle: radial coordinates from an interior point, scaled by the distance to the boundary in each direction, give such a homeomorphism. Conjugation therefore gives the same fixed-point assertion on the disk. If r were a continuous retraction from the unit disk to its boundary, define F(x)=−r(x). A fixed point would have ∣x∣=1, hence r(x)=x and x=−x, impossible on the unit circle. Thus no continuous disk-to-boundary retraction exists. The continuous conclusion has been deduced from the grid parity argument, not used to prove it.

Solution

Words: 490
12G OurBigBook.com
In the hyperbolic-ball model, the limit set of a Kleinian group is the boundary accumulation set of an orbit Go of an interior point: Λ(G)=Go∩∂H3. The choice of o does not matter, since any two such orbits remain a fixed hyperbolic distance apart. It is closed and G-invariant. The complicated/non-elementary hypothesis excludes relatively compact groups and elementary groups with at most two limit points; in particular the limit set is nonempty. Having no finite boundary orbit alone would not exclude a compact rotation group, whose interior orbits are bounded.
If Λ(G) were finite and nonempty, the orbit of any of its points would be a finite boundary orbit, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus it is infinite. In fact it cannot be countable. We give the essential minimality/perfectness argument. A sequence of Möbius transformations sending an interior point toward ξ∈Λ has a subsequence converging on the boundary away from one exceptional point to the constant ξ. This follows by normalizing the representing 2×2 matrices: a diverging sequence has a rank-one projective limit, with one kernel line and one image line. For any boundary point η, the absence of a finite orbit allows choosing h∈G with hη different from that exceptional point; then gj​hη→ξ. Hence the orbit of every η∈Λ is dense in Λ.
If ξ were an isolated limit point, density of every orbit would make every point belong to its orbit: each orbit must hit the open singleton {ξ}. Every point would then be isolated by equivariance, making the compact set Λ discrete and therefore finite, a contradiction. Thus Λ is a nonempty perfect compact metric space. Repeatedly choosing two disjoint smaller neighbourhoods meeting this perfect set, with diameters tending to zero, associates distinct nested limits to all infinite binary sequences. The limit set is therefore uncountable.
Jorgensen inequality states that for a non-elementary discrete group generated by lifts A,B∈SL(2,C),
∣tr2A−4∣+∣tr(ABA−1B−1)−2∣≥1.
(28)
For a concrete failure of discreteness, take A=diag(es/2,e−s/2) and B=(1−1​10​) with s>0 small. The fixed points of A and of BAB−1 collectively include 0,∞,−1, so the group is non-elementary. Direct multiplication gives both summands equal to 4sinh2(s/2). Their sum is less than one when s is sufficiently small, proving this two-generator group is not discrete.
For a connected-limit-set example, the modular group generated by z↦z+1 and z↦−1/z is discrete because its matrices have integer entries. It preserves the upper half-plane; its limit set is the extended real line, a circle. Indeed the orbit of the parabolic fixed point infinity consists of the rational points and infinity, dense in that circle. For a disconnected example, choose four pairwise disjoint round disks and two loxodromic maps pairing the exterior of each negative disk with the interior of its positive disk. The Schottky group generated by these maps is free and discrete by the disjoint-domain ping-pong construction. Successive reduced words give nested disjoint disks with shrinking diameters; their limiting points form a Cantor set. Thus its limit set is disconnected, unlike that of the modular group.

The data are read row by row into a vector of 84 prices. The first factor cycles through the six goods within each row; the second repeats each of the fourteen resort levels for six entries. Thus the linear regression fits one observation per resort-good cell, after taking natural logarithms. With treatment coding, its underlying statistical model is
logPij​=α+ri​+gj​+εij​,r1​=g1​=0,εij​ independent N(0,σ2),
(29)
for resorts i=1,…,14 and goods j=1,…,6. This is an additive two-way analysis of variance on log prices, equivalently a multiplicative resort/goods model on the price scale, with no interaction. There are 1+13+5=19 fitted parameters and 84−19=65 residual degrees of freedom​.
In a balanced complete table, the fitted log price is the resort row mean plus the goods column mean minus the grand mean. Thus every resort coefficient is its row mean minus the Algarve row mean, and every goods coefficient is its column mean minus the meal column mean. The intercept is the fitted mean log price for a meal in Algarve, not necessarily the observed log price in that cell. Exponentiating coefficients gives price multipliers: the beer coefficient corresponds to approximately e−2.1084=0.1214 times the meal scale, and car hire to e2.8016=16.47 times that scale. Likewise the Sorrento resort effect gives a common factor e0.5981=1.819 relative to Algarve, if the no-interaction model is valid.
The standard errors are computed from s2(XTX)−1 with s=0.3425. Balance gives goods-contrast standard error s2/14​=0.1295 and resort-contrast standard error s2/6​=0.1978. Each reported t statistic is its estimated coefficient divided by its standard error. Under the Gaussian model and the corresponding zero-coefficient null, it has a Student t-distribution with 65 degrees of freedom; the reported probabilities are two-sided tail probabilities. All goods contrasts are strongly significant, largely reflecting unlike goods and units of purchase. Among the resort contrasts, Costa del Sol, Majorca, Florida, Sorrento, Sicily and Madeira have unadjusted probabilities below 0.05. This is six separate comparisons with Algarve, not a simultaneous ranking guarantee or an omnibus test of all resorts. Multiple comparisons and model adequacy must be considered before declaring a universal cheapest resort.
The residual standard error measures variation on the log scale; e0.3425≃1.408 is a typical multiplicative one-standard-deviation factor. Under the lognormal distribution, exp(α+ri​+g​j​) estimates the conditional median/geometric mean price, while the arithmetic mean has the additional factor exp(σ2/2). The reported R2=0.962 means 96.2 percent of the observed log-price sum of squares around its overall mean is explained. It does not mean resorts alone explain that fraction, nor that 96.2 percent of variation on the original price scale is explained.
With only one observation per cell, unrestricted goods-by-resort interactions cannot be estimated separately from residual error. The model assumes comparable quoted items, approximately common log-error variance, independent errors and common resort multipliers across goods. Residuals can reveal failures, such as a particular resort having unusually costly taxis but ordinary prices for other goods. The intercept's test against zero concerns a fitted baseline geometric price of one pound; it is not an assessment of the overall model's validity.

Zorn lemma states that a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound contains a maximal element. To prove it from the axiom of choice and Hartogs theorem, suppose no element were maximal. Fix a choice function on the nonempty subsets of the poset. Every chain then has a strict upper bound: choose an upper bound, and, since it is not maximal, choose an element strictly above it. Let κ be a Hartogs ordinal which cannot inject into the poset. By transfinite recursion for α<κ, choose a strict upper bound xα​ of all previously chosen xβ​, β<α; for the empty initial chain choose any element. The previous elements form a chain at every stage. The resulting strictly increasing sequence injects κ into the poset, contradicting Hartogs. Hence a maximal element exists. Choice is used in fixing the function selecting a strict upper bound at every successor and limit stage; Hartogs and transfinite recursion themselves do not supply those selections.
Apply Zorn lemma to the linearly independent subsets of R over Q, ordered by inclusion. A chain's union is linearly independent because any finite linear relation is contained in one member of the chain. A maximal independent set B must span R, since otherwise one could append a vector outside its span. Thus B is a rational-vector-space basis of R.
It is infinite: a finite-dimensional rational vector space is countable, whereas R is not. If its cardinal is κ, finite rational linear combinations show ∣R∣=max(ℵ0​,κ); uncountability forces κ=∣R∣. A basis of R2 is (B×{0})∪({0}×B), where these expressions mean the vectors (b,0) and (0,b). Its cardinal is κ+κ=κ, using the infinite-cardinal arithmetic available under choice. A bijection between the two bases extends uniquely by finite rational linear combinations to a linear bijection. Therefore
R≅Q​R2.​
(40)
This is an algebraic isomorphism, with no assertion of continuity or real-linearity.

For the first assertion, use the standard nonempty finite-graph convention. Choose a longest simple path in an acyclic graph. Its endpoint can have no neighbour outside the path, or the path could be extended; it can have no neighbour farther back than the adjacent path vertex, or there would be a cycle. Its degree is therefore at most one. The qualification matters for infinite graphs: a two-sided infinite path is acyclic and every vertex has degree two.
A finite tree with n>1 has a leaf by this argument and connectedness. Removing it and its one edge leaves a tree with n−1 vertices. Induction from the one-vertex tree proves a tree of order n has n−1 edges. Conversely, a finite connected graph has a spanning tree: begin with one vertex and repeatedly add an edge to a new vertex until every vertex is reached. This creates no cycle and uses n−1 edges. If the original graph has exactly that many edges, it equals its spanning tree and is itself a tree.
To embed a tree T of order t, root it and list its vertices so every nonroot vertex follows its parent. Embed the root at any vertex of G. When embedding a new vertex, at most t−2 neighbours of its parent's image are already used, while that image has degree at least t−1. An unused neighbour exists and can be chosen. This constructs an injective edge-preserving copy of T, so
δ(G)≥t−1 ⟹ T⊆G.​
(41)
For t≥2, the complete graph Kt−1​ has minimum degree t−2 but too few vertices to contain T. Thus the degree bound cannot be lowered in general. A subgraph copy need not be induced; extra edges in G do not obstruct the construction.

An element x of an extension L/K is an algebraic element over K when some nonzero polynomial in K[t] vanishes at x. Let its monic minimal polynomial have degree d. Polynomial division shows K[x] is spanned by 1,x,…,xd−1, and minimality makes these vectors independent. The minimal polynomial is irreducible; for any nonzero q(x), Bezout's identity between q and that polynomial gives a polynomial representative for q(x)−1. Thus K[x] is a field, equals K(x), and has degree d.
Conversely, if K(x) has finite vector-space dimension d, then 1,x,…,xd are linearly dependent over K, giving a nonzero annihilating polynomial. Hence
x algebraic over K ⟺ [K(x):K]<∞.​
(42)
An algebraic extension is one in which every element is algebraic. Suppose M/L and L/K are algebraic, and take α∈M. A polynomial relation for α over L uses only finitely many coefficients a1​,…,ar​. Each is algebraic over K, so adjoining them successively gives a finite extension E=K(a1​,…,ar​), by the proved criterion and the tower law. The same relation makes α algebraic over E, so E(α)/E is finite. Therefore E(α)/K is finite, and its subspace K(α) is finite-dimensional. The criterion makes α algebraic over K. Since α was arbitrary, M/K is algebraic.

Without that assumption, the disjoint union of two tori mapping by the identity on each component is a covering of the torus and is none of the three listed connected spaces. The correct general statement classifies each connected component; here is the intended connected proof.
The universal cover is R2→R2/Z2=T, and π1​(T)=Z2. In the supremum-norm metric, S is totally bounded if for every ε>0 finitely many norm balls of radius ε cover it. It is uniformly bounded if some M satisfies ∣f(x)∣≤M for all f∈S,x∈K. It is equicontinuous if for each x∈K and ε>0 there is a neighbourhood U of x with ∣f(y)−f(x)∣<ε for all f∈S,y∈U. This definition works for compact Hausdorff K without assuming it is metrizable.
Suppose S is totally bounded. A finite radius-one net makes ∥f∥∞​ uniformly bounded by one plus the largest norm of a net centre. For equicontinuity, choose a finite ε/3 net. Continuity of each centre gives a common neighbourhood of x on which all centre values vary by less than ε/3. Approximating any f by its centre and using the triangle inequality at x and y bounds its variation by ε. Thus both conditions follow.
Conversely suppose those two conditions hold. For each x, choose a neighbourhood Ux​ on which every function varies from its value at x by less than ε/3. Compactness provides a finite cover Ux1​​,…,Uxm​​. The vectors (f(x1​),…,f(xm​)) form a bounded subset of Cm, so partition their possible values into finitely many boxes of diameter less than ε/3 in the maximum-coordinate norm. From each occupied box choose one function as a representative. If f and its representative h have sample values in the same box, and y∈Uxj​​, then
∣f(y)−h(y)∣≤∣f(y)−f(xj​)∣+∣f(xj​)−h(xj​)∣+∣h(xj​)−h(y)∣<ε.
(52)
These finitely many representatives are a norm net, proving total boundedness is equivalent to uniform boundedness and equicontinuity. This supplies the finite-net part of the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem directly.
For a bounded set that is not totally bounded, take the standard unit vectors S={en​:n≥1} in the Banach space ℓ2. Their norms are one and their pairwise distances are 2​. A ball of radius less than 2​/2 contains at most one of them, so finitely many such balls cannot cover S.

If two candidates existed, their difference would extend to an entire doubly periodic function: the principal parts cancel at every possible pole. It is bounded on a fundamental parallelogram, hence on the plane, so Liouville theorem makes it constant. The local O(z) difference tends to zero, making the constant zero. Thus the function is unique.
The function z↦℘(−z) has the same periodicity, poles and local estimate. Uniqueness therefore proves ℘(−z)=℘(z). Its Laurent expansion is consequently
℘(z)=z−2+c2​z2+c4​z4+⋯,

It therefore has exactly two, proving

A pi-system is a collection closed under finite intersections. The uniqueness theorem says that two probability measures agreeing on a generating pi-system agree on its generated sigma-field. For finite measures one also fixes the total mass; for a sigma-finite version one requires a covering sequence from the pi-system with finite common masses. Adding the whole space to a pi-system of events causes no change to its generated sigma-field and preserves the stated independence condition.
Fix H∈H. On σ(G) the finite measures A↦P(A∩H) and A↦P(A)P(H) agree on G and on the whole space. Uniqueness makes them agree for every A∈σ(G). Now fix such an A. On σ(H) the measures B↦P(A∩B) and B↦P(A)P(B) agree on H and the whole space; a second application of uniqueness proves
P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)(A∈σ(G), B∈σ(H)).​
(60)
Thus the two generated sigma-fields are independent. The extension is done one argument at a time, not by assuming the required independence for arbitrary unions.
For the independent random variables, let G be the rectangles ⋂i=1m​{Yi​∈Bi​} and let H be the analogous rectangles in the Zj​. Both are pi-systems. Joint independence of the full list factors each combined rectangular probability into the product of the individual probabilities, hence into P(G)P(H). Their generated sigma-fields are exactly σ(Y1​,…,Ym​) and σ(Z1​,…,Zn​). The proved result therefore gives independence of the two vector-generated sigma-fields.

(k2+q2)2=4k2pq,(2−s2)2=41−s2​1−κs2​,s=c/cS​, κ=cS2​/cP2​.​
(107)
For such a root, one can choose A=0 and B=−2ikpA/(k2+q2), providing the requested wave explicitly. Squaring and excluding the static zero root gives the equivalent Rayleigh polynomial
s6−8s4+(24−16κ)s2−16(1−κ)=0,0<s<1.
(108)
The physical positive root is unique as allowed in the question. All factors of k cancel in the speed equation, so the Rayleigh surface wave is nondispersive, with c determined only by the material constants. The potentials decay exponentially over depths of order k−1.

a OurBigBook.com
Write h=Δx, k=Δt=μh, and D0​u=[u(x+h)−u(x−h)]/(2h). The scheme is the trapezoidal time rule with a centered spatial derivative:
un+1−un=2k​(D0​un+1+D0​un).
(109)
Insert a smooth exact solution of ut​=ux​. Taylor expansion of the unnormalized one-step residual gives
u(t+k)−u(t)2k​(D0​u(t+k)+D0​u(t))​=kut​+21​k2utt​+61​k3uttt​+O(h4),=kux​+21​k2uxt​+41​k3uxtt​+61​kh2uxxx​+O(h4).​
(110)
All repeated time derivatives equal the corresponding spatial derivatives. The first two orders cancel, leaving
R=−(12k3​+6kh2​)uxxx​+O(h4)=−12μ(μ2+2)​h3uxxx​+O(h4).​
(111)
Thus the one-step local error is O(h3) at fixed Courant number. If “local truncation error” is instead defined after division of the residual by Δt, its order is O(h2); these are two different normalizations of the same second-order method.

Solution

Words: 75
b OurBigBook.com
For the Fourier mode umn​=gneimξ, substitution gives
(1−2iμ​sinξ)g=1+2iμ​sinξ,g=1−iμsinξ/21+iμsinξ/2​.​
(112)
The denominator is never zero for real μ,ξ, and numerator and denominator are complex conjugates, so ∣g∣=1. Parseval's identity therefore makes each step norm-preserving on square-summable grid data. The method is von Neumann stable for every μ>0, with no upper Courant restriction. It is an implicit nondissipative scheme; unconditional stability does not remove phase error or guarantee accuracy at a large time step.
